listenings.text: Hi there. Marcus Feld, I am with Aperture Clearing out of Chicago. I run the bank partnerships side, so I have spent the last four years talking to exactly the kind of people who are in this hall today. We have been live in eleven markets since twenty twenty-two, and Brazil is the one my board asks me about every single quarter. I have just come from the settlement panel, which was better than I expected. What brings you here?

Morning. Priya Sandhu, head of product at Levenford Rail. We are London based, and I have been in payments for about twelve years now, mostly on the infrastructure side rather than the customer side. We have not launched in Latin America yet, which is honestly the reason I am here. I have already had three conversations this morning with people who tell me the same thing about settlement times, so I am starting to think there is a pattern. Have you been to this conference before?

Good morning. My name is Rohit Menon, and I am with Cardinal Systems in Bangalore. I look after our correspondent banking product. We have worked with about forty banks since the company started, and I have personally been on this product for six years. This is my third time at this conference, and I have to say the questions people ask have changed completely. Two years ago everybody wanted to talk about cost. Now everybody wants to talk about speed.

the first sentence you use to start talking to a stranger

paras: Nobody arrives at a conference speaking their best English. Marta Oliveira, who has run the international desk of a Portuguese bank since two thousand and fifteen, says it took her four years to admit that. “For a long time I thought I was slower than the others,” she says. “Then I noticed the pattern. On the first morning I understood about half of what people said to me. By the second afternoon I understood almost everything. Nothing about my English had changed in thirty hours. Something about my ear had.”

So she stopped fighting it and started using it. She now treats the first two hours as a warm-up, on purpose, and she protects them. She arrives early, she queues at the registration desk instead of using the fast lane, and she talks to whoever is next to her while she waits for her badge. None of those conversations matter. That is the point. “A queue is the cheapest English lesson at any conference,” she says. “Nobody is selling anything, nobody is judging your grammar, and if you lose a sentence you just ask again.”

She has two or three opening lines she uses every time, and she has not changed them in years. Is this your first time here? Where have you come in from? What have you seen so far that was worth it? The third one is her favourite, because it is a real conversation starter: it gives the other person something to talk about, and it tells her, in one answer, which sessions are worth her afternoon.

The lanyard does some of the work for her. She reads it while she shakes hands, so she never has to ask for a company name twice, and she has learned to say the name back immediately. On the networking floor she keeps the session schedule open on her phone, not to follow it exactly, but so that she always has a reason to end a conversation politely.

Twice, she says, this habit has produced something. She once ran into the head of a German clearing house in the coffee queue on the first morning, twenty minutes before either of them had said a serious word to anybody. That conversation became a partnership. “I did not plan it and I could not have planned it,” she says. “But I was warm, and he was not. That was the whole difference.”
reading.source: A composite portrait of a conference regular, written for this lesson.
